cells.C: How Your Dissertation Spine Would Be Classified

Your spine would be viewed as a theory-informed, interpretive, process-oriented conceptual research architecture. Its theoretical center is stakeholder theory, operationalized through the stakeholder-salience attributes of power, legitimacy, and urgency (PLU). It uses PLU to explain how stakeholder prioritization moves through decision rights, escalation pathways, and evidence-acceptance mechanisms to shape recoverability assurance.

The spine as a whole is not one theory. It integrates an established theoretical foundation, an operational theoretical lens, governance constructs, a proposed process model, a qualitative methodology, and an analytical method.

This dissertation employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Using PLU as sensitizing concepts, the study interpretively examines the process through which stakeholder prioritization shapes decision rights, escalation pathways, evidence standards, and recoverability assurance in U.S. SMEs using or adopting ITDRPaaS. The SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship constitutes a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established substantive theory.

cells.C: The Primary Classification: Middle-Range Explanatory Theory
If you were required to select one principal theoretical classification, your spine would most closely reflect a:
Middle-range, interpretive, process-oriented explanatory application of stakeholder-salience theory.

It is middle-range because stakeholder-salience theory addresses a bounded organizational phenomenon: how managers prioritize stakeholders according to perceived PLU attributes. It does not attempt to explain every element of organizational behavior or disaster recovery.

It is explanatory because your study is not merely identifying which stakeholders possess power, legitimacy, or urgency. It seeks to explain how perceived salience influences governance actions and produces consequences for recoverability assurance. The central explanatory movement is:
Mitchell et al. (1997) provide the established salience explanation; your dissertation applies and potentially refines that explanation in the bounded context of U.S.-SME ITDRPaaS governance.
The Spine as a Process-Mechanistic Explanation
Your spine is especially strong as a process-mechanistic model because it specifies how one theoretical condition may become organizational action.
Organizational actors perceive that stakeholder claims possess varying degrees of power, legitimacy, and urgency.
Those perceptions shape managerial attention and stakeholder priority.
Prioritization influences who receives, activates, challenges, or overrides decision authority.
Decision rights determine whether an issue is escalated, when escalation occurs, and who receives it.
Authorized actors determine what recovery evidence is considered sufficient.
Accepted, repeatable, and auditable evidence supports recoverability assurance.
Testing, disruptions, corrective actions, and organizational learning may feed back into future stakeholder assessments and governance arrangements.

This formulation is more theoretically developed than a simple linear chain because it identifies the activities connecting the constructs. Process theory explains how events unfold, while mechanistic theory specifies the entities and activities producing an outcome (Van de Ven & Poole, 1995).
A more complete representation is therefore:
A["Stakeholder claims and PLU perceptions"] --> B["Priority and decision rights"]
E --> F["Testing, learning, and corrective action"]
The feedback loop is important. Your spine should not imply that SAL → DR → ESC → AE always operates as a fixed, uninterrupted sequence. An incident may cause:
a lowered or heightened evidence threshold;
Thus, the spine is process-oriented but recursive, not strictly linear or deterministic.
Your spine is principally interpretive and explanatory, not statistically predictive. The study asks how IT/network managers and other governance actors perceive and interpret:

PLU functions as a set of sensitizing concepts. It directs attention toward theoretically relevant conditions without forcing all participant accounts into predetermined PLU categories. This distinction is essential because stakeholder salience depends partly on managerial perception: a stakeholder may possess formal authority, contractual legitimacy, or an urgent claim, but organizational consequences depend on whether decision makers recognize and act on those attributes.

Your qualitative design could identify recurring expectations, but it should not claim that PLU predicts recoverability outcomes across all SMEs. Instead, findings would appropriately be described as:
extending the theory into a new domain;
contradicting part of the proposed explanation.

cells.C: The study should not be labeled fully multilevel theory unless it explicitly explains how processes at one level influence processes at another. At present, “primarily meso-level with micro, interorganizational, and macro influences” is the more defensible description.
Your spine does not claim that stakeholder urgency or power produces the same governance result in every organization. It assumes that effects may depend on contextual conditions.

The influence of stakeholder urgency on escalation may depend on decision-rights clarity, incident severity, executive availability, provider dependence, regulatory exposure, and the criticality of the affected service.

Therefore, your spine should be described as contingency-sensitive, not universalistic.
Is Your Spine a Substantive Theory?

Your spine has the potential to produce a substantive theoretical explanation of ITDRPaaS governance, but the proposed SAL → DR → ESC → AE model should not currently be called a substantive theory. Before making that claim, the empirical study would need to:
trace the relationships through participant and artifact evidence;
identify the mechanism connecting the constructs;
investigate negative cases and rival explanations;
assess feedback and recursive relationships; and
If the findings consistently substantiate the model, the final dissertation might claim that it has:

developed a bounded substantive explanation of how stakeholder-salience dynamics become translated through decision rights, escalation pathways, and evidence-acceptance practices into recoverability assurance within participating U.S. SMEs.
That is still more calibrated than claiming the study “created and proved a new theory.”
What the Spine Is—and Is Not

cells.D: A grand theory of disaster recovery

cells.C: Bounded to U.S. SMEs and ITDRPaaS

The study’s theoretical spine constitutes a middle-range, interpretive, and process-oriented application of stakeholder-salience theory. PLU functions as the operational lens through which the study examines how stakeholder prioritization shapes decision rights, escalation pathways, evidence acceptance, and recoverability assurance in U.S. SMEs using or adopting ITDRPaaS.

The proposed study employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Power, legitimacy, and urgency function as sensitizing concepts for examining how organizational actors interpret and prioritize competing recovery claims. The study conceptualizes stakeholder prioritization as operating through decision-rights allocation, escalation pathways, exception authority, and evidence-acceptance practices that collectively shape recoverability assurance. Accordingly, the SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship is positioned as a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established theory. Through generic qualitative inquiry, critical-incident prompts, reflexive analysis, and interview–artifact triangulation, the study will examine whether empirical evidence supports, refines, extends, complicates, or contradicts the proposed governance-to-assurance mechanism.
Your spine would be viewed most accurately as:

A stakeholder-theory-grounded, PLU-operationalized, middle-range explanatory spine that uses an interpretive, process-mechanistic, primarily meso-level, and contingency-sensitive conceptual model to investigate how stakeholder salience is translated through governance mechanisms into recoverability assurance in U.S.-SME ITDRPaaS contexts.

The short answer is that the spine is not itself a finished theory. It is a theory-informed conceptual and methodological architecture capable of producing a bounded substantive theoretical contribution after empirical analysis.

cells.D: As we enter Week 4, we're focusing on qualitative research methods and their analytical processes. This week, you'll choose one of the major qualitative approaches—Case Study, Phenomenology, Delphi, or Grounded Theory—and explore its analytical process through the literature.
Steps to Prepare for This Week's Discussion and Assignment:

Select one of the approved qualitative methods for your research: Case Study, Phenomenology, Delphi, or Grounded Theory. Think about your interests and how the chosen approach aligns with your research goals.

Begin your literature search by looking for seminal works that detail the analytical process for your chosen method. Key databases like Google Scholar, JSTOR, or your institution's library can be invaluable resources.
Pay particular attention to foundational texts and influential authors in the field. These works will provide you with a solid understanding of the methodology and its application.

As you review the literature, take note of the specific terminology used in your chosen approach. For example, if you select Grounded Theory, familiarize yourself with concepts like "open coding," "axial coding," and "theoretical sampling."

Then, compare this terminology with that found in the Generic Thematic Analysis of Qualitative Data document. Identify any similarities or differences in the terms used, and consider how these terms reflect the methodologies' unique focuses.

Investigate the assumptions that underpin your chosen qualitative approach. For instance, phenomenology emphasizes understanding participants' lived experiences, while case studies focus on in-depth exploration of specific instances.
Contrast these assumptions with those associated with Generic Thematic Analysis. Consider how these foundational beliefs influence the research process and the interpretation of data.

As you gather information, synthesize your findings into a coherent understanding of your chosen approach. Be prepared to discuss how the analytical processes, terminology, and assumptions compare to those in Generic Thematic Analysis.

Formulate your thoughts and insights based on your research. Think about how you can contribute to the discussion and what questions you might want to pose to your peers regarding their experiences with qualitative methodologies.

By following these steps, you will be well-prepared for this week’s discussion and assignment. Engaging deeply with the literature will enhance your understanding of qualitative research methods and their application in your own work.
Looking forward to an engaging week of exploration and discussion!
